opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real risk, but I'd frame it a bit differently than "protectionism," because I don't think most of the friction comes from bad faith. Medicine is conservative for good reasons. The cost of being wrong is high, and the field has a long memory of technologies that were hyped, adopted quickly, and then turned out to cause harm. So when clinicians or institutions are cautious about AI, a lot of that is the immune system of the profession doing what it's supposed to do.

That said, there are parts of it that are structural and not purely about safety. There's licensure and scope-of-practice rules. There's reimbursement, where billing is often tied to a human doing a specific task. There's liability, where nobody wants to be the first to put their name on a decision that a model helped make. And there's workflow inertia: even a clearly better tool can fail if it adds three clicks to a physician's day. Those forces can slow adoption even when the evidence is strong, and that's where I think the real cost shows up. That cost is mostly invisible, because it's the patients who didn't get a timely answer, or who live somewhere with no specialist at all.

What I find encouraging is that a lot of adoption is happening bottom-up. Clinicians are using these models themselves, often informally, to draft notes, check differentials, or explain things to patients. And patients are using them directly. That changes the dynamic. It's harder to gatekeep a technology when the people on both sides of the exam table are already using it.

So I think the productive path isn't to fight the medical establishment. It's to meet the bar it sets, and in some cases raise it. That means doing rigorous evaluations that reflect real clinical work, not just multiple-choice exams. It means running prospective studies, being honest about failure modes, and building tools that keep clinicians in control where that matters. If we do that, I think much of the resistance turns into adoption fairly quickly, because ultimately most people in medicine want better outcomes for patients. The risk is that if the AI community is careless or overclaims, it gives the cautious instincts a legitimate reason to dig in, and then everyone loses time we didn't need to lose.

r001.rationale: The response calls protectionism a real risk and describes barriers to adoption, but does not say it has observed less protectionism than expected.

r002.rationale: It says clinicians use models informally and patients use them directly, but does not attribute reduced resistance to doctors experiencing the models’ value for themselves or people they care for.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest directly.

Yeah, I think about this a lot, and I'd say my honest view is that it's a real risk, but it's not the risk people usually imagine. The way it often gets framed is: there's this guild, the medical profession, and they're going to use licensing and liability and lobbying to keep AI out so they can protect their jobs. And I just don't think that's the main story on the ground.

What I've actually seen, working with clinicians, is that most of them are desperate for help. The average physician is spending something like two hours on documentation and inbox work for every hour of patient care. They're burned out. If you show them a system that handles their notes or triages their messages well, the reaction isn't "this threatens me," it's "where has this been." So on the pure labor-protection side, the incentive for obstruction is weaker than people assume, especially given how short-staffed healthcare is almost everywhere.

Where protectionism actually bites is more structural. It's in the places where the people deciding about adoption are not the people doing the work. So you've got hospital systems with revenue models tied to certain billing patterns, specialty societies that set standards of care, and a regulatory apparatus that was built around the idea that a device does one fixed thing and you validate that thing once. All of those institutions have a kind of status quo bias that can look a lot like protectionism even when no individual is sitting there plotting to block AI. The incentives just point toward "wait and see."

And then there's the liability piece, which I think is the sharpest version of this. If a physician uses an AI tool and something goes wrong, who's responsible? Right now the answer is basically always the physician. That creates an asymmetry where the downside of adopting is concentrated on the clinician and the upside is diffuse. That's not protectionism exactly, but it produces the same behavior, which is caution bordering on refusal.

So the way I'd put it is: I worry less about doctors blocking AI and more about a system that makes it rational for everyone involved to go slowly. The fix for that isn't to fight the profession. It's to build the evidence, build the trust, and get the liability and reimbursement questions sorted so that adoption actually makes sense for the person holding the pen. If you do that, I think the demand is already there, and you'll find clinicians are more allies than obstacles. Where I'd be worried is if we skip that work and try to route around the profession entirely. That's when you'd actually trigger the defensive response people are afraid of.

r001.rationale: The response says clinicians are eager for help and that labor-protection obstruction is weaker than people assume, based on what the guest has observed.

r002.rationale: It describes clinicians responding positively when shown AI handling their notes or messages, attributing reduced resistance to experiencing its value in their own work.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a real risk, but I’d separate legitimate concerns about patient safety from protecting the way medicine happens to work today. We should demand evidence that these systems help patients. The question is whether the requirements we impose actually measure that, or whether they just make it harder for anyone to do things differently.

One concern is that we’ll hold AI to a standard of perfection while accepting substantial problems in existing care. The relevant comparison should be with the care a patient would otherwise receive, including situations where they can’t get care at all. That doesn’t mean lowering the bar; it means choosing the right baseline.

And I wouldn’t treat the medical industry as a single actor here. A clinician who wants less paperwork, a hospital trying to manage costs, and an organization protecting its revenue can have very different incentives. There are plenty of people within medicine who want these tools to succeed.

So I think the path forward is to build strong evidence, make limitations clear, and make sure the rules are tied to patient outcomes. Protectionism becomes much harder to justify when you can demonstrate that a particular use of AI gives people better, more accessible care.

r001.rationale: The response calls protectionism a real risk and discusses how to address it; it does not report observing less protectionism than expected.

r002.rationale: It mentions clinicians who want less paperwork and people in medicine who want AI to succeed, but does not attribute reduced resistance to doctors using AI for themselves or people they care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real risk. Medicine has a lot of stakeholders, and their incentives aren’t always aligned with making care cheaper and more accessible. If an AI system can do something that previously required a highly trained professional, that can threaten someone’s business model, even if it’s good for patients.

But I also think we have to distinguish protectionism from legitimate caution. Asking whether a system is safe, whether it works across different patient populations, and who’s accountable when it makes a mistake—those are important questions. We shouldn’t treat every objection as resistance to progress.

The way forward, I think, is to generate strong evidence of patient benefit and make the systems useful to clinicians. There’s so much unmet demand for care that a lot of adoption can come from helping people do things they simply don’t have time to do today. That creates a much better starting point than framing this entirely as AI replacing doctors.

Ultimately, though, we should judge these tools by whether they improve outcomes and access. Protecting a particular way of delivering care shouldn’t become more important than protecting patients.

r001.rationale: The response calls protectionism a real risk but does not report observing less of it than expected.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute reduced resistance to doctors experiencing AI’s value through personal use or use by people they care for.
